claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can be homogenized into a high-temperature BCC phase.
Phase stability of the high-temperature BCC state is governed by competition between thermodynamic driving forces and kinetic constraints.
The relevant thermodynamic driving force is the free-energy difference between BCC and lower-temperature phases.
Sluggish constituent-element diffusion delays transformation of the BCC phase.
Al diffusion is particularly sluggish and the presence of Al enhances the kinetic barrier to transformation.
Transformation is triggered when the thermodynamic incentive to form equilibrium phases overcomes the diffusion-controlled kinetic barrier.
The controlled comparison is isothermal annealing near the predicted transformation temperature for varying durations versus rapid quenching from the same temperature.
The selected annealing temperatures should have a free-energy difference that is only marginally favorable for transformation.
Cooling profile, atmosphere, and grain size must be controlled to isolate diffusion kinetics from thermodynamic driving forces.
Local atomic ordering and diffusion-limited clustering act as precursors to the emerging equilibrium phase.
The precursor ordering or clustering is mediated particularly by Al enrichment at specific lattice sites.
At high temperatures, the BCC state is kinetically stabilized by sluggish diffusion despite a modest thermodynamic drive for transformation.
During holding at an intermediate temperature, local compositional fluctuations and ordering progressively lower the transformation barrier.
Once diffusion permits sufficient atomic rearrangement, the thermodynamic driving force promotes nucleation and growth of a lower-temperature phase.
Isothermally annealed samples will initially retain the BCC structure.
After a critical incubation time, isothermally annealed samples will develop a precipitate, an ordered phase, or another transformation product.
Rapidly quenched samples will retain the BCC state and exhibit no phase transformation.
The proposed mechanism applies only near a critical transformation temperature where the interphase free-energy difference is marginal.
At temperatures above or below that regime, different diffusion behavior or inherent BCC instability may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
A lack of statistically significant time-dependent transformation or precursor ordering in annealed samples relative to quenched controls would falsify the hypothesis.
